sections.learning_objective: Turn a small scenario into functional requirements and explicit limits.
sections.markdown: Start with the job a small system must do, not a collection of fashionable components. A functional requirement describes a user-visible action. A constraint limits the solution, such as using one school computer. A quality requirement describes a property that can be checked, such as an agreed response-time target under a stated workload. Put the boundary around what this version owns.

sections.markdown: A small club needs a shared equipment notebook. Members can view items and a volunteer can mark an item borrowed or returned. The first version serves 20 members on a local network; payments and public sign-up are out of scope. A simple browser → local service → database path is enough to discuss initially. Before choosing a cache or queue, ask whether a measured problem needs one. If two people request one item at the same moment, the borrowing rule needs an explicit consistency decision; drawing more boxes does not decide it.

sections.markdown:
Guided: 'Members can see which items are available' is functional. 'Works on the existing local computer' is a constraint. Independent: define a minimal attendance notebook, list two actions, one limit and one failure case.

<details><summary>Illustrative review, not the only correct design</summary>Record attendance and view a day's list; serve one classroom on the local network; retain a saved record after a restart. Decide whether repeat marks update a record or are rejected. Other coherent boundaries can be valid.</details>

Revision: name the users, state actions, record limits, make success observable, identify failures and exclude tempting extras. Open designs use a rubric; Forge does not automatically judge arbitrary architecture prose.
